roman.title: The Roman Empire
roman.intro: Across the Mediterranean, at the end of Trajan’s reign.
roman.note: Select provinces directly on the map. Boundaries are approximate reconstructions for ca. AD 117 from Harvard’s DARMC, based on the Barrington Atlas. Coastlines and rivers use modern Natural Earth geometry for orientation.

places.name: Roma
places.fact: The imperial capital stood on the Tiber. Trajan’s forum celebrated the emperor whose conquests brought the empire to its widest extent.

places.name: Londinium
places.fact: Roman Londinium grew around a crossing of the Thames, linking river traffic with roads across Britannia.

places.name: Carthago
places.fact: Rebuilt under Roman rule after the destruction of Punic Carthage, this Mediterranean city became a major centre of Roman Africa.

places.name: Alexandria
places.fact: This Mediterranean port connected Egypt’s Nile valley with the wider Roman world. Egypt had been under Roman rule since 30 BC.

places.name: Antiochia
places.fact: Antioch on the Orontes was a leading city in Roman Syria, near routes linking the Mediterranean with inland Asia.

places.name: Ephesus
places.fact: A major city of the Roman province of Asia, Ephesus lay near the Aegean coast in western Anatolia.

places.name: Britannia
places.modern: Much of present-day England and Wales
places.fact: The Roman province occupied part of Britain. The island’s northern regions remained beyond direct Roman provincial rule.

places.name: Hispania Baetica
places.fact: Baetica occupied the south of the Iberian Peninsula. This marker represents the province rather than a city.

places.name: Gallia Lugdunensis
places.fact: One of the provinces of Roman Gaul, named for Lugdunum, modern Lyon. Its geography does not match a modern national border.

places.name: Aegyptus
places.fact: Rome governed Egypt as a province. The Nile valley was central to its agriculture and connections with the Mediterranean.

places.name: Dacia
places.fact: Trajan’s Dacian conquests added territory north of the Danube to Roman rule in the early second century.

places.name: Africa Proconsularis
places.modern: Mainly present-day Tunisia and adjacent areas
places.fact: This Roman province faced Italy across the central Mediterranean. Its provincial name did not mean the entire continent of Africa.

sceneSymbols.label: Roman eagle standard
sceneSymbols.note: Modern drawing inspired by documented Roman military emblems. The colours and complete arrangement are illustrative, not a recovered ancient flag.

sceneSymbols.label: SPQR banner
sceneSymbols.note: Modern decorative banner using the Roman-state abbreviation. No claim is made that this complete design survives from antiquity.

symbolObjects.label: Eagle and standards · 82 BC coin
symbolObjects.note: C. Valerius Flaccus denarius. The reverse depicts a legionary eagle between two military standards. It is evidence for the emblems, not for the colours of a national flag.
symbolObjects.credit: Hamburger Kunsthalle, ID235. Photograph: Martin Ziegert. Public Domain Mark 1.0.

medieval.title: The Middle Ages
medieval.intro: Kingdoms, empires and cities of the high medieval world.
medieval.scope: Europe, North Africa and the eastern Mediterranean
medieval.note: Select mapped realms directly. Boundaries are approximate reconstructions around AD 1200 from Harvard’s DARMC. Some later polities in the source layer are omitted. Coastlines and rivers provide modern geographic orientation; medieval sovereignty was often overlapping or disputed.

places.name: Kingdom of England
places.fact: Around 1200, England was ruled by the Plantagenet dynasty. King John’s reign began in 1199; Magna Carta followed in 1215.

places.name: Kingdom of Scotland
places.fact: Scotland was a separate kingdom in this period. Its medieval political history should not be read through the later United Kingdom.

places.name: Kingdom of France
places.fact: Royal authority and the power of regional lords overlapped in medieval France. A single location marker cannot represent all its changing frontiers.

places.name: Holy Roman Empire
places.fact: A complex empire of principalities and other territories in central Europe. It was distinct from the ancient Roman Empire.

places.name: Byzantine Empire
places.fact: In AD 1200 Constantinople was still the Byzantine imperial capital. The Fourth Crusade captured it in 1204, after this expedition’s reference date.

places.name: Almohad Caliphate
places.modern: North Africa and part of Iberia
places.fact: The Almohads ruled across parts of North Africa and southern Iberia around 1200. Their architecture connected both shores of the western Mediterranean.

places.name: London
places.fact: London stood within the Plantagenet kingdom of England, whose rulers also held lands across the English Channel.

places.name: Paris
places.fact: Paris was an important royal and intellectual centre in medieval France. The period saw growing royal authority and urban life.

places.name: Venice
places.fact: Venice was a maritime republic linked to Mediterranean trade. Its ships would play a central role in the Fourth Crusade after 1200.

places.name: Constantinople
places.fact: The city on the Bosporus linked Europe and Asia. Its medieval inhabitants considered themselves Romans; “Byzantine” is a later historical label.

places.name: Toledo
places.fact: Toledo was a major city of Christian-ruled Iberia by 1200, within a peninsula of several kingdoms and Islamic states.

places.name: Palermo
places.fact: Palermo was an important centre of the Kingdom of Sicily, where Latin, Greek and Arabic cultural traditions had interacted.

sceneSymbols.label: England · three lions
sceneSymbols.note: Three gold lions on red belong to the royal arms used by Richard I near the end of the twelfth century. This is a modern graphic rendering, not a surviving cloth.
sceneSymbols.credit: Yaddah / Brunanburh, Wikimedia Commons, public-domain release.

sceneSymbols.label: France · semé-de-lis
sceneSymbols.note: France ancien used a field scattered with fleurs-de-lis. A scholarly study discusses its twelfth-century origins and the banner described at Bouvines in 1214.

symbolObjects.label: Almohad banner · early 1200s
symbolObjects.status: Surviving textile · dated 1212–1250 in the cited catalogue
symbolObjects.note: The so-called Las Navas de Tolosa banner is preserved at Las Huelgas, Burgos. The catalogue dates this textile after the c.1200 map snapshot; its traditional battle association should not be treated as a secure capture history.
symbolObjects.credit: Las Huelgas textile; image via Wikimedia Commons, Las Navas de Tolosa banner2.jpg, public-domain reproduction. Catalogue: Al-Andalus (1992), p.326.

symbolObjects.label: Abbasid black banner
symbolObjects.note: Black banners are documented in Abbasid political symbolism. This graphic represents the colour only; its dimensions and plain layout are illustrative, without invented inscriptions.
symbolObjects.credit: Original Atlas graphic. Evidence: The black flag of the Abbasids, Gladius 20 (2000), DOI 10.3989/gladius.2000.71.

symbolObjects.label: Hospitaller white-cross banner
symbolObjects.note: The Order of Malta traces a white cross on red to a decree of 1130, recorded by its historian Giacomo Bosio in 1594. This is a modern rendering of that tradition, not a surviving twelfth-century cloth.

symbolObjects.label: Jerusalem cross · heraldic banner
symbolObjects.status: Modern rendering · arms documented on a c.1250–75 object
symbolObjects.note: The Met holds a thirteenth-century basin bearing the kingdom’s large cross and smaller crosses. This banner translates the heraldic motif into a modern illustration; it is not evidence for this exact flag in 1200.

symbolObjects.label: Marinid banner · 1339–1340
symbolObjects.note: Sultan Abu al-Hasan’s banner was made in Fes in 1339–1340 and is preserved in Toledo Cathedral. It belongs to a later Islamic dynasty and is shown for comparison, not as an Almohad or Ayyubid flag.
symbolObjects.credit: Toledo Cathedral textile. Reproduction from Louvre exhibition catalogue Maroc medieval, pp.546–547, via Wikimedia Commons; public-domain reproduction.

events.text: Pope Urban II called for the First Crusade.
Crusader forces captured Jerusalem.
The Second Crusade failed to take Damascus.
Salah al-Din took Jerusalem.
The Third Crusade left Crusader forces holding Acre and Cyprus.
The Fourth Crusade captured Constantinople.
Acre fell to Mamluk forces, ending the main Crusader foothold on the mainland.

timelineGroups.title: The Ayyubids · 1171–1250
timelineGroups.note: Ayyubid branches did not all disappear in 1250; this endpoint concerns Egypt.

events.text: Salah al-Din established the Ayyubid sultanate in Egypt.
Ayyubid control extended into Yemen.
Salah al-Din expanded his power in Syria.
Jerusalem passed to Salah al-Din’s rule.
Mamluks overthrew independent Ayyubid rule in Egypt.
The Almohads took Marrakesh from the Almoravids.
Almohad power included Seville, Córdoba and other Iberian cities.
Work on the Hasan Mosque in Rabat remained unfinished.
Defeat at Las Navas de Tolosa weakened Almohad power in Iberia.
The conventional endpoint of the Almohad period.

timelineGroups.title: Seljuqs of Rum · 1071–1243
timelineGroups.note: This was not the immediate end of the dynasty; later Seljuq rulers continued under Mongol power.

events.text: The Seljuq victory at Manzikert opened Anatolia to further Turkic settlement.
A Seljuq branch established rule from Nicaea and became known as the Seljuqs of Rum.
The Latin capture of Constantinople altered the Anatolian balance of power.
The reign of Kay Qubad I saw strong commercial and artistic activity.
Defeat at Köse Dagh brought the Seljuqs under Mongol overlordship.

timelineGroups.note: Baghdad and Iraq are historical context here; they are outside this map’s Mediterranean territory coverage.

events.text: The Abbasids replaced the Umayyad caliphate.
Baghdad was founded as the new capital.
The court moved to Samarra.
The court returned from Samarra to Baghdad.
The Mongol conquest ended the Baghdad Abbasid caliphate.

republic.title: The Roman Republic.
republic.caption: ROMAN REPUBLIC · 60 BC
republic.intro: Before Caesar’s Gallic campaigns. Discover 18 cities and 13 regions across the Republican Mediterranean.
republic.note: A 60 BC snapshot from AWMC. Select broad geographic regions; groupings are learning aids, not exact provincial boundaries. Italia and Cisalpine Gaul are grouped together. Small islands are grouped with nearby regions.

places.name: Italia & Cisalpine Gaul
places.fact: The Republic was governed from Rome. This broad map group includes peninsular Italy and Cisalpine Gaul, which were administratively distinct in 60 BC.

places.name: Hispania
places.fact: Rome held much of the Iberian Peninsula by 60 BC, but the northern interior remained outside its control. This group combines the mapped Republican holdings rather than later imperial provinces.

places.name: Sicilia
places.fact: Sicily was one of Rome’s earliest overseas provinces. Its central Mediterranean position connected Italy with Africa.

places.name: Africa
places.fact: The Republican province of Africa occupied a much smaller area than the continent bearing the same name. The map shows Roman holdings in 60 BC.

places.name: Asia
places.fact: The province called Asia lay in western Anatolia. Its name referred to a Roman province, not the entire modern continent.

places.name: Syria
places.modern: Syria and neighbouring eastern Mediterranean lands
places.fact: Syria formed part of Rome’s eastern holdings by 60 BC. The Republic’s territory already stretched far beyond Italy before the age of Augustus.

places.name: Roma
places.fact: Rome was the political centre of the Republic. Assemblies, magistrates and the Senate shaped a state whose power expanded across the Mediterranean.

places.name: Syracusae
places.fact: Syracusae stood on Sicily’s southeastern coast. Find the island territory that contained this ancient Greek city under Roman rule.

places.name: Utica
places.fact: Utica lay on the North African coast, near the former city of Carthage. Find the Republic’s African territory, rather than the entire continent.

places.name: Tarraco
places.fact: Tarraco stood on the northeastern coast of Roman Hispania. Its location faced the Mediterranean routes linking Iberia and Italy.

places.name: Ephesus
places.fact: Ephesus lay near the Aegean coast of Anatolia, within the Roman province of Asia. Find the western Anatolian territory.

places.name: Antiochia
places.fact: Antiochia lay inland from the northeastern Mediterranean coast. Locate it within the mapped Syrian territory of the late Republic.

places.name: Transalpine Gaul
places.fact: Transalpine Gaul lay beyond the Alps from Rome’s perspective. This map shows the southern Roman holdings in 60 BC, before Caesar’s campaigns farther north.

places.name: Macedonia & Greece
places.fact: The map combines Macedonia and Greece as a broad geographic learning region. These lands had long histories of Greek cities and Macedonian kingdoms before Roman rule.

places.name: Corsica
places.fact: Corsica is the northern of the two large islands west of peninsular Italy. It is kept separate from Sardinia here for geographic practice, rather than as a claim about provincial administration.

places.name: Bithynia & Pontus
places.fact: This learning region covers the mapped Roman holdings along northern Anatolia. The Black Sea lies to the north; the Aegean coast and the province of Asia lie to the southwest.

places.name: Sardinia
places.fact: Sardinia lies south of Corsica and west of Italy. Its position made it part of the central Mediterranean world connecting Roman Italy, Sicily and North Africa.

places.name: Cyrenaica
places.fact: Cyrenaica occupied the Mediterranean coast of northeastern Africa. Its city of Cyrene gave the region its name; the mapped territory is distinct from the Republic’s province of Africa farther west.

places.name: Crete
places.fact: Crete is the long island south of mainland Greece. It appears as a separate selectable island here, even though Roman administration linked it with Cyrenaica.

places.name: Ostia
places.fact: Ostia developed near the mouth of the Tiber. Its earliest archaeologically documented fortified settlement dates to the fourth century BC; as Rome expanded, the town’s commercial role grew.

places.name: Pompeii
places.fact: Pompeii became a Roman colony in 80 BC, twenty years before this map’s date. Its famous burial by Vesuvius in AD 79 still lay far in the future.

places.name: Narbo Martius
places.fact: Narbo Martius was founded in 118 BC as Rome’s first colony in Gaul. Locate it in the southern Roman holdings, rather than the much larger Gallic territory of the later Empire.

places.name: Pergamon
places.fact: Pergamon rose above the Bakırçay plain in western Anatolia. A major Hellenistic city before Roman rule, its remains preserve the layered history of this Aegean region.

places.name: Cyrene
places.fact: Cyrene began as a Greek colony and became one of the great cities of the Hellenic world. Find its region on the North African coast, across the Mediterranean from Crete.

places.name: Athenae (Athens)
places.fact: The Acropolis preserves the monumental legacy of classical Athens, including the Parthenon. These fifth-century BC buildings were already centuries old at the time of this Republican map.

places.name: Gortyna (Gortys)
places.fact: Gortyna became the capital of the Roman province of Crete and Cyrenaica. The quiz separates Crete and Cyrenaica into geographic regions, so choose the island containing the city.

places.name: Carthago Nova
places.fact: Carthago Nova stood on the southeastern coast of Iberia. Its name means “New Carthage”; do not confuse this Spanish city with Carthage on the African coast.

places.name: Caralis
places.fact: Caralis corresponds to modern Cagliari on southern Sardinia. Archaeological finds reveal a city with a long history before, during and after Roman rule.

places.name: Aleria
places.fact: Aleria was an ancient settlement on Corsica’s eastern side, with Greek and later Roman phases. Its archaeological remains help trace the island’s connections with the wider Mediterranean.

places.name: Panormus
places.fact: Panormus is ancient Palermo, on Sicily’s northern coast. The city’s Punic and Roman past predates the much later medieval buildings for which Palermo is also known.

places.name: Agrigentum (Akragas)
places.fact: Founded as a Greek colony in the sixth century BC, the city became a major Mediterranean centre. Its Doric temples remain a reminder of Sicily’s Greek heritage alongside its later Roman history.

insignia.alt: Illustrative burgundy and gold SPQR banner
insignia.label: SPQR · Roman Republic
insignia.note: Modern illustration, not a verified ancient national flag. The same Roman-state emblem is used across these territories. SPQR means “The Senate and People of Rome”.

background.label: Government
background.text: A republic governed through magistrates, the Senate and citizen assemblies. Political power was unequal; expansion brought wealth, conflict and pressure on these institutions.

background.label: Languages · wider Roman world
background.text: Latin was Rome’s language. Greek also connected many communities of the eastern Mediterranean; local languages continued alongside these shared languages.

background.label: Religion · varied local traditions
background.text: Roman worship involved many gods, public ceremonies and household observances. Greek and other Mediterranean traditions influenced Roman practice; beliefs differed between communities.

timeline.text: Traditional beginning of the Republic after Rome’s monarchy.
Wealthy plebeians had gained political equality with patricians.
The snapshot used for this expedition.
Julius Caesar was assassinated after civil wars and his dictatorship.
Octavian received the title Augustus, marking the conventional start of the imperial period.

crusades.title: The Muslim world during the Crusades.
crusades.caption: MUSLIM-RULED MEDITERRANEAN · c. AD 1200
crusades.intro: Three dynasties, many cities. Explore the Almohads, Ayyubids and Seljuqs of Rum after the Third Crusade.
crusades.note: Mediterranean focus, not the entire Muslim world: Abbasid Iraq, Iran, Arabia and lands farther east are outside this edition. DARMC polygons are generalized and incomplete, with major gaps in Morocco and Iberia; city dots show individual locations. Borders are approximate, and Muslim rule did not imply a uniformly Muslim population.

places.name: Almohad Caliphate
places.fact: The Almohads were an Amazigh (Berber) dynasty governing lands across North Africa and al-Andalus. Marrakesh was their North African centre of power; Seville was their capital in al-Andalus.

places.name: Ayyubid Sultanate
places.modern: Egypt and parts of the Levant
places.fact: Salah al-Din (Saladin), a Kurdish ruler, established Ayyubid power in Egypt in 1171 and extended it into Syria. Around 1200, different branches of his family governed major centres.

places.name: Seljuq Sultanate of Rum
places.fact: The Seljuqs of Rum were a Turkic dynasty whose realm drew on Persianate Islamic and local Byzantine traditions. Rum referred to the Roman past of these lands; the dynasty was distinct from the Ayyubids.

places.name: Cairo
places.fact: Cairo was a major Ayyubid centre. Its citadel belongs to the fortification programme associated with Salah al-Din; the dynasty also sponsored religious and artistic building projects.

places.name: Alexandria
places.fact: Alexandria lies on Egypt’s Mediterranean coast, west of the Nile delta. In this expedition it is placed within the Ayyubid Egyptian realm shown by the historical map.

places.name: Damascus
places.fact: Damascus was an important Ayyubid court and cultural centre. Patronage supported buildings and crafts as well as political power, within a region contested by several ruling families.

places.name: Aleppo
places.fact: Aleppo was another major Ayyubid centre. The citadel’s early thirteenth-century development illustrates how rulers combined fortification with monumental architecture.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.fact: Salah al-Din took Jerusalem in 1187. The city was under Muslim rule around 1200; control changed again later in the thirteenth century. Its sacred places mattered to Muslims, Christians and Jews.

places.name: Konya (Iconium)
places.fact: Konya was the capital of the Seljuqs of Rum. Their mosques, madrasas and palaces drew on Persianate Islamic traditions while reflecting Anatolia’s diverse cultural heritage.

places.name: Sivas
places.fact: Sivas became an important centre of Seljuq monumental architecture. Its celebrated thirteenth-century buildings largely postdate this map’s approximate 1200 snapshot.

places.name: Seville (Ishbiliya)
places.fact: Seville was the Almohad capital in al-Andalus. The great mosque and its minaret, now known as the Giralda, demonstrate the dynasty’s architectural patronage.

places.name: Córdoba (Qurtuba)
places.fact: Córdoba was among the Iberian cities held by the Almohads in the twelfth century. Al-Andalus had its own history and political struggles, far from the Levantine Crusader states.

places.name: Tunis
places.fact: Tunis lies on the North African shore of the Mediterranean. This map groups it with the Almohad holdings; later Hafsid rule belongs to a different political phase.

background.label: Government
background.text: These were distinct dynastic states, not a single Muslim empire. Ayyubid family courts, Almohad caliphs and Seljuq sultans ruled different territories.

background.label: Religion and communities
background.text: Muslim rulers governed religiously diverse populations. In Anatolia, Islamic traditions interacted with Byzantine and Armenian Christian heritage.

background.label: Beyond warfare
background.text: Courts also sponsored architecture, education and crafts. Almohad centres in Marrakesh and Seville supported Islamic learning and geometric decoration.

viking.title: The Viking Age
viking.intro: Trading ports, northern kingdoms and the journeys that connected them.
viking.note: Historical boundaries are approximate DARMC reconstructions. This European map explores the wider Viking Age, not a single Viking empire. City questions include trading sites whose heyday predates AD 1000. North Atlantic settlements are outside this map’s coverage.

places.name: Hedeby
places.fact: At the narrow neck of Jutland, Hedeby connected routes between the North Sea and the Baltic. Its harbour, streets and nearby Danevirke defences preserve evidence of a major Viking Age trading centre.

places.name: Birka
places.fact: Birka and nearby Hovgården reveal the trading networks of Viking Scandinavia. Birka flourished chiefly in the eighth to tenth centuries; this is an earlier Viking Age site on the AD 1000 context map.

places.name: Ribe
places.fact: Ribe was one of the town-like trading centres of Viking Scandinavia. Such settlements linked craft production and exchange across sea routes.

places.name: Kaupang
places.fact: Kaupang, also associated with the name Skiringssal, was a Norwegian trading centre. It belongs to the earlier Viking Age network rather than a modern national capital.

places.name: Jelling
places.fact: The burial mounds, rune stones and church at Jelling illustrate Denmark’s transition toward Christianity and royal consolidation in the tenth century.

places.name: Jórvík / York
places.fact: Scandinavian settlement transformed York into an important urban centre. By the map’s date it belonged to the English kingdom; the Viking Age question recalls its earlier Scandinavian connections.

places.name: Dyflin / Dublin
places.fact: A Viking fortified base was established at Dublin in 841. By the tenth century it was among the ports developing into Ireland’s first towns.

places.name: Rouen
places.fact: Normandy took its name from Scandinavian settlers. Their descendants became part of the Christian political world of western Europe rather than remaining a single overseas Viking state.

places.name: Novgorod
places.fact: Novgorod belonged to the eastern trading world linking Scandinavia with river routes into Rus’. The Viking Age extended through commerce and settlement as well as raiding.

places.name: Kyiv
places.fact: Kyiv was a major centre of Rus’. Scandinavian travellers formed part of a much wider eastern European world, whose societies cannot be reduced to a Viking colony.

places.name: Denmark
places.modern: Approximate historical territory; see the dated map note.
places.fact: Danish royal power grew during the Viking Age. Jelling provides physical evidence of tenth-century kingship and Christianization.

places.name: Norway
places.modern: Approximate historical territory; see the dated map note.
places.fact: Norway’s coasts connected communities by sea. Kaupang was one of the trading centres in the Scandinavian network.

places.name: Sweden
places.modern: Approximate historical territory; see the dated map note.
places.fact: The Swedish region included trading networks represented by Birka and Hovgården. Viking Age Scandinavia was politically varied, not one unified empire.

places.name: Normandy
places.modern: Approximate historical territory; see the dated map note.
places.fact: Scandinavian settlement in northern France helped form Normandy. Its later rulers participated in the Christian aristocratic culture of western Europe.

places.name: Kingdom of England
places.modern: Approximate historical territory; see the dated map note.
places.fact: The AD 1000 map shows an English kingdom after the earlier Scandinavian settlement of places such as York. Viking Age raids, settlement and changing rule were distinct processes.

places.name: Kyivan Rus’
places.modern: Approximate historical territory; see the dated map note.
places.fact: Rus’ linked eastern European communities and long-distance river trade. Norse travellers were one part of its diverse history.

background.label: More than raiders
background.text: The Viking Age included farming, craft production, exchange, settlement and violence. Scandinavian societies were diverse; the shaded realms are historical context, not a single Viking empire.

background.label: Reading this map
background.text: Political context is ca. AD 1000. Earlier trading sites are retained as questions so you can explore the whole Viking Age.

timeline.text: The broad Viking Age: Scandinavian journeys, settlement and exchange.
A Viking fortified base is established at Dublin.

renaissance.title: The Renaissance
renaissance.intro: Cities of art, commerce and learning in a changing Europe.
renaissance.note: Historical boundaries are approximate DARMC reconstructions. The map is dated ca. 1450, before the fall of Constantinople. Italian city-states are not separately resolved in this source: Florence and Milan sit within its broad Holy Roman Empire context, not a claim of direct imperial control. Facts may discuss later Renaissance developments, with dates stated.

places.name: Florence
places.fact: Florence became a leading centre of Renaissance art and humanist learning. Its classical revival was supported by patrons including the Medici; the map source groups this area broadly rather than drawing the Florentine state.

places.name: Venice
places.fact: Venice joined maritime commerce with a distinctive artistic culture. Its Renaissance painting developed across the fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries.

places.name: Rome
places.fact: Rome’s ancient buildings and texts helped inspire Renaissance study. The papal city later drew major artistic and architectural commissions; those later projects should not be mistaken for completed works in 1450.

places.name: Milan
places.fact: Milan was a major northern Italian court city. This source’s broad imperial polygon does not resolve its duchy as an independent selectable state.

places.name: Naples
places.fact: Naples was the centre of a southern Italian kingdom. Renaissance culture developed among competing courts and city-states, not within a unified Italian nation.

places.name: Rimini
places.fact: Alberti’s Tempio Malatestiano at Rimini, begun around 1450, reinterpreted the forms of Roman temple architecture.

places.name: Paris
places.fact: Paris was a royal and intellectual centre. Renaissance ideas circulated across Europe at different times; the cultural label does not mean every region changed in the same year.

places.name: London
places.fact: London was England’s royal and commercial centre. This early Renaissance map predates the Tudor dynasty and the later Elizabethan cultural flowering.

places.name: Lisbon
places.fact: Lisbon connected Portugal to Atlantic routes. The fifteenth century’s maritime expansion formed part of the wider world in which Renaissance Europe developed.

places.name: Constantinople
places.fact: In this ca. 1450 snapshot, Constantinople remains Byzantine. Its Ottoman conquest occurred in 1453, a crucial distinction when reading the map.

places.name: Edirne
places.fact: Edirne was an Ottoman centre in the European Balkans. The Ottoman state was part of the Renaissance-era Mediterranean world, not outside its geography.

places.name: Mainz
places.fact: Mainz is associated with Gutenberg’s printing enterprise. The Gutenberg Bible appeared in the 1450s, shortly after this map’s approximate date.

places.name: Republic of Venice
places.modern: Approximate historical territory; see the dated map note.
places.fact: Venice governed a maritime republic and territories around the Adriatic and eastern Mediterranean. Its source polygon is a broad historical reconstruction.

places.name: Papal States
places.modern: Approximate historical territory; see the dated map note.
places.fact: The pope exercised territorial rule in central Italy. Rome also became a major centre of Renaissance patronage.

places.name: Kingdom of France
places.modern: Approximate historical territory; see the dated map note.
places.fact: France was a kingdom within a politically divided Europe. The ca. 1450 snapshot belongs near the end of the Hundred Years’ War.

places.name: Kingdom of Portugal
places.modern: Approximate historical territory; see the dated map note.
places.fact: Portugal was a separate kingdom on the Atlantic edge of Europe. Its overseas expansion belongs to the broader fifteenth-century setting.

places.name: Ottoman Empire
places.modern: Approximate historical territory; see the dated map note.
places.fact: The Ottoman state held lands in Anatolia and the Balkans. Constantinople remains outside its territory in this pre-1453 snapshot.

places.name: Kingdom of Naples
places.modern: Approximate historical territory; see the dated map note.
places.fact: Southern mainland Italy formed a kingdom distinct from the Papal States and northern Italian political centres.

background.label: A cultural movement, many states
background.text: Renaissance Europe contained courts, kingdoms, republics and city-states. Humanist study and artistic experimentation spread unevenly across these political boundaries.

background.label: A dated snapshot
background.text: Boundaries represent ca. 1450. Constantinople has not yet fallen to the Ottomans; later artistic achievements are described with their dates. Italian city-state boundaries are generalized in this map source.
